claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and spatial distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Fine, homogeneously distributed precipitates promote toughness.
Fine precipitates promote toughness by mediating dislocation motion and impeding crack propagation.
Coarse or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates cause early crack initiation and embrittlement.
The proposed initial as-cast alloy has a near-random elemental distribution and little or no secondary-phase precipitation.
A moderately elevated-temperature aging treatment of suitable duration can nucleate fine precipitates without significant coarsening.
An inert aging atmosphere avoids oxidation.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy composition ranges that support stable secondary-phase formation and have sufficiently limited interdiffusional kinetics.
Precipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution are the structural mediators of toughness.
Fine precipitates act as effective dislocation-pinning points.
Fine precipitates encourage crack deflection and thereby dissipate mechanical energy during deformation.
Overaging or suboptimal thermal conditions can produce coarse or unevenly distributed precipitates.
Coarse or unevenly distributed precipitates can act as crack-initiation sites and reduce toughness.
Aged samples with fine, uniformly distributed precipitates will have greater fracture toughness than the as-cast baseline.
Samples with larger or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates will have lower toughness.
The as-cast baseline has minimal precipitation and a relatively uniform but unrefined microstructure.
The hypothesis is limited to aging temperature and time ranges that avoid excessive precipitate coarsening.
Changing aging temperature and time can systematically control precipitate size and distribution.
TEM or atom-probe tomography can quantify the precipitate characteristics relevant to the hypothesis.
A lack of systematic association between precipitate refinement and increased toughness, or equal or greater toughness in coarse or inhomogeneous conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.
